reference.source: Williams Hematology / Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
clinicalPearls: An acquired clonal disorder of haematopoietic stem cells caused by somatic PIGA mutation, not an inherited condition
Loss of the GPI anchor removes the complement regulators CD55 and CD59 from blood cells, leaving red cells vulnerable to complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis
The classic triad is intravascular haemolytic anaemia, cytopenias from associated marrow failure, and a marked predisposition to thrombosis, often at unusual sites
Flow cytometry using FLAER and antibodies to GPI-anchored proteins is the diagnostic gold standard, having replaced the older Ham acidified serum test
Haemoglobinuria classically produces dark morning urine, and free haemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, contributing to dystonia, abdominal pain, and pulmonary hypertension
Thrombosis, frequently venous and in sites such as the hepatic or cerebral veins, is the leading cause of death
Complement C5 inhibition markedly reduces intravascular haemolysis and thrombotic risk, and allogeneic transplantation is reserved for marrow failure or refractory disease
reference.pathophysiology: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the X-linked PIGA gene within a haematopoietic stem cell, so it is a clonal but non-inherited disorder. PIGA is required for the first step in synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor that tethers many proteins to the cell surface. Loss of GPI anchoring strips the affected cells of the complement-regulatory proteins CD55 and CD59, which normally protect them from complement attack. Unopposed activation of the alternative complement pathway on red cells causes chronic intravascular haemolysis, releasing free haemoglobin that depletes nitric oxide and drives smooth-muscle dystonia and pulmonary hypertension. The PIGA-mutant clone often expands in the setting of immune-mediated marrow injury (as in aplastic anaemia), and complement activation on platelets and endothelium underlies the characteristic thrombotic tendency.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of intravascular haemolysis (microangiopathy, mechanical, march haemoglobinuria)
Unexplained venous thrombosis, including Budd-Chiari syndrome
Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and other complement-mediated disorders
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood flow cytometry with FLAER and GPI-anchored protein markers on multiple lineages
Full blood count, reticulocytes, and blood film to assess haemolysis and cytopenias
Haemolysis panel including lactate dehydrogenase, bilirubin, haptoglobin, and urinary haemosiderin
Bone marrow examination and cytogenetics to evaluate associated marrow failure or dysplasia
Iron studies, as chronic urinary iron loss can cause deficiency
Imaging for suspected thrombosis at typical and atypical sites
redFlags: Thrombosis, especially hepatic, portal, cerebral, or other unusual-site venous events
Severe haemolytic crisis with profound anaemia and haemoglobinuria
Progressive pancytopenia indicating evolving marrow failure
Features of pulmonary hypertension or renal impairment from chronic haemolysis
reference.prognosis: The course is variable and can be chronic; thrombosis remains the major cause of mortality, but complement C5 inhibition has substantially improved survival and quality of life, and marrow failure or clonal evolution influences the long-term outlook.
pitfalls: Assuming PNH is an inherited disease rather than an acquired clonal PIGA disorder
Attributing thrombosis to other causes and failing to test for PNH in unusual-site venous thrombosis
Overlooking a small PNH clone in patients with aplastic anaemia or myelodysplasia
Missing iron deficiency from chronic urinary haemoglobin and haemosiderin loss
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
